Caribbean
The Caribbean is a geo-political region in the middle of the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color> centered around the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Sea</color> in the <color=#3366CC>North</color>
<color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color>, mostly overlapping with the West Indies. Bordered by <color=#3366CC>North America</color> to the north and also the west
through <color=#3366CC>Central America</color>, and <color=#3366CC>South America</color> to the south, it comprises numerous islands, cays, islets, reefs, and
banks.
It includes the <color=#3366CC>Lucayan Archipelago</color>, Antilles of the West Indies; the Quintana Roo islands and Belizean islands of the
<color=#3366CC>Yucatán Peninsula</color>; and the Bay Islands, Miskito Cays, Archipelago of San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina,
Corn Islands, and San Blas Islands of Central America. It also includes the coastal areas on the continental mainland of
the Americas bordering the region from the Yucatán Peninsula in North America through Central America to the
<color=#3366CC>Guianas</color> in South America.
Overview
Situated largely on the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean plate</color>, the region has thousands of islands, <color=#3366CC>islets</color>, <color=#3366CC>reefs</color>, and cays. Island arcs
delineate the northern and eastern edges of the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Sea</color>: the <color=#3366CC>Greater Antilles</color> in the north and the <color=#3366CC>Lesser</color>

<color=#3366CC>Antilles</color>, which includes the <color=#3366CC>Leeward Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Windward Islands</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Leeward Antilles</color>, to the east and south. The
nearby northwestern <color=#3366CC>Lucayan Archipelago</color>, comprising <color=#3366CC>The Bahamas</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Turks and Caicos Islands</color>, and the island
of <color=#3366CC>Barbados</color> in the Lesser Antilles, are considered to be a part of the Caribbean despite not bordering the Caribbean
Sea. All the islands in the Antilles, including the Lucayan Archipelago, form the West Indies, a term often
interchangeable with the Caribbean. The <color=#3366CC>archipelago of Bermuda</color> is not part of the Caribbean, as it lies in the <color=#3366CC>Sargasso</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sea</color> to the north, but it is an associate member of the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Community</color>.
On the continental mainland of the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>, the Caribbean coasts of <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>, Central America, and South America,
including the <color=#3366CC>Yucatán Peninsula</color> of Mexico, Bay Islands Department of <color=#3366CC>Honduras</color>, the Mosquitia region, <color=#3366CC>Cartagena</color> and

<color=#3366CC>Barranquilla</color> in <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Maracaibo</color> and Cumaná in <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>, are considered part of the Caribbean. As with the
coastal areas of the mainland, <color=#3366CC>Guyana</color>, <color=#3366CC>Suriname</color>, and <color=#3366CC>French Guiana</color>, even if they do not border the Caribbean Sea,
are often completely included within the Caribbean due to their strong <color=#3366CC>political</color> and <color=#3366CC>cultural</color> ties with the region.
Geopolitically, the islands of the Caribbean are often regarded as a subregion of <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, though sometimes
they are included in Middle America, or regarded as its own subregion as the Caribbean. The Caribbean is sometimes
considered alongside Central America as a region.
Generally, the Caribbean region is organized into 33 political entities, including 13 <color=#3366CC>sovereign states</color>, 12 <color=#3366CC>dependencies</color>,
7 <color=#3366CC>overseas territories</color>, and various <color=#3366CC>disputed territories</color>. From 15 December 1954 to 10 October 2010, there was a
territory known as the <color=#3366CC>Netherlands Antilles</color> composed of five islands, all of which were <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color> dependencies. From 3
January 1958 to 31 May 1962, there was also a short-lived political union called the British West Indies Federation
composed of ten English-speaking Caribbean territories, all of which were then British dependencies.
The modern Caribbean is one of the most ethnically diverse regions on the planet, as a result of <color=#3366CC>European colonization</color>

by the <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color>, <color=#3366CC>English</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>, and <color=#3366CC>French</color>; the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color> from <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>; <color=#3366CC>indentured servitude</color> from the <color=#3366CC>Indian</color>
<color=#3366CC>subcontinent</color> and East Asia; as well as modern immigration from around the world.
Etymology and pronunciation
The region takes its name from the <color=#3366CC>Caribs</color>, an Amerindian ethnic group historically present in the <color=#3366CC>Lesser Antilles</color> and
parts of adjacent South America that the <color=#3366CC>Spanish colonists</color> named the region after at the time of the <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>conquest of the Americas</color>.
The two most prevalent pronunciations of "Caribbean" outside the Caribbean are, with the primary <color=#3366CC>stress</color> on the third
<color=#3366CC>syllable</color>, and, with the stress on the second. Most authorities of the last century preferred the stress on the third
syllable. This is the older of the two pronunciations, but the stressed-second-syllable variant has been established for
over 75 years. It has been suggested that speakers of <color=#3366CC>British English</color> prefer while North American speakers more
typically use, but major American dictionaries and other sources list the stress on the third syllable as more common in
<color=#3366CC>American English</color> too. According to the American version of Oxford Online Dictionaries, the stress on the second
syllable is becoming more common in UK English and is increasingly considered "by some" to be more up to date and
more "correct".
The Oxford Online Dictionaries claim the stress on the second syllable is the most common pronunciation in the
Caribbean itself, but according to the Dictionary of Caribbean English Usage, the most common pronunciation in
Caribbean English stresses the first syllable instead,.
Definition
The word Caribbean has multiple uses. Its principal ones are geographical and political. The Caribbean can also be
expanded to include territories with strong cultural and historical connections to Africa, <color=#3366CC>slavery</color>, <color=#3366CC>European colonisation</color>
and the plantation system.
• The United Nations geoscheme for the Americas presents the Caribbean as a distinct region within the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>.
• Physiographically, the Caribbean region is mainly a chain of islands surrounding the Caribbean Sea. To the north,
the region is bordered by the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of Mexico</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Straits of Florida</color> and the Northern <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color>, which lies to
the east and northeast. To the south lies the coastline of the <color=#3366CC>continent</color> of <color=#3366CC>South America</color>.
History
The oldest evidence of humans in the Caribbean is in southern <color=#3366CC>Trinidad</color> at Banwari Trace, where remains have been
found from 7,000 years ago. These pre-ceramic sites, which belong to the Archaic (pre-ceramic) age, have been
termed Ortoiroid. The earliest archaeological evidence of human settlement in <color=#3366CC>Hispaniola</color> dates to about 3600 BC, but
the reliability of these finds is questioned. Consistent dates of 3100 BC appear in <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color>. The earliest dates in the
<color=#3366CC>Lesser Antilles</color> are from 2000 BC in <color=#3366CC>Antigua</color>. A lack of pre-ceramic sites in the <color=#3366CC>Windward Islands</color> and differences in
technology suggest that these Archaic settlers may have Central American origins. Whether an Ortoiroid colonization of
the islands took place is uncertain, but there is little evidence of one.
<color=#3366CC>DNA</color> studies changed some of the traditional beliefs about pre-Columbian indigenous history. According to <color=#3366CC>National</color>
<color=#3366CC>Geographic</color>, "studies confirm that a wave of pottery-making farmers—known as Ceramic Age people—set out in
canoes from the northeastern coast of South America starting some 2,500 years ago and island-hopped across the
Caribbean. They were not, however, the first colonizers. On many islands they encountered a foraging people who
arrived some 6,000 or 7,000 years ago ... The ceramicists, who are related to today's Arawak-speaking peoples,
supplanted the earlier foraging inhabitants—presumably through disease or violence—as they settled new islands."
Between 400 BC and 200 BC, the first ceramic-using agriculturalists, the Saladoid culture, entered Trinidad from South
America. They expanded up the Orinoco River to Trinidad, and then spread rapidly up the islands of the Caribbean.
Some time after 250 AD another group, the Barancoid, entered Trinidad. The Barancoid society collapsed along the
Orinoco around 650 AD and another group, the Arauquinoid, expanded into these areas and up the Caribbean chain.
Around 1300 AD a new group, the Mayoid, entered Trinidad and remained the dominant culture until Spanish
settlement.
At the time of the European discovery of most of the islands of the Caribbean, three major Amerindian indigenous

peoples lived on the islands: the <color=#3366CC>Taíno</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Greater Antilles</color>, <color=#3366CC>The Bahamas</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Leeward Islands</color>; the <color=#3366CC>Island</color>
<color=#3366CC>Caribs</color> and Galibi in the Windward Islands; and the Ciboney in western Cuba. The Taínos are subdivided into Classic
Taínos, who occupied <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color> and part of Hispaniola; Western Taínos, who occupied the Bahamian archipelago,
Cuba, <color=#3366CC>Jamaica</color>, and part of Hispaniola; and the Eastern Taínos, who occupied the northern <color=#3366CC>Lesser Antilles</color>. The
southern Lesser Antilles, including <color=#3366CC>Martinique</color> and <color=#3366CC>Trinidad</color>, were inhabited by both Carib-speaking and
Arawak-speaking groups.
European contact
<color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> arrived in the Caribbean on the island of Hispaniola in 1492. Soon afterward, both Portuguese
and Spanish explorers began claiming territories in Central and South America. These early colonies brought gold to
Europe; most specifically England, the Netherlands, and France. These nations hoped to establish profitable colonies
in the Caribbean. Colonial rivalries made the Caribbean a battleground for European wars for centuries.
In 1512, after pressure from Dominican friars, the Laws of Burgos were introduced by the Spanish Crown to better
protect the rights of the New World natives. The Spanish used a form of slavery called the <color=#3366CC>Encomienda</color>, where slaves
would be awarded to the conquistadors, who were charged with protecting and converting their slaves. This had a
devastating impact on the population, so starting in 1503, slaves from Africa were imported to the colony. <color=#3366CC>Jamaica</color> was

ceded to <color=#3366CC>England</color> by <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> while both <color=#3366CC>Martinique</color> and the western third of <color=#3366CC>Hispaniola</color> were ceded to <color=#3366CC>France</color>.
While early slave traders were Portuguese and Spanish, known as the First Atlantic System, by the 17th century the
trade became dominated by British, French, and Dutch merchants. This was known as the Second Atlantic System. 5
million African slaves would be taken to the Caribbean, and around half would be traded to the British Caribbean
islands. Slavery was abolished first in the Dutch Empire in 1814. Spain abolished slavery in its empire in 1811, with the
exceptions of Cuba, Puerto Rico, and Santo Domingo. Slavery was not abolished in Cuba until 1886. Britain abolished
the slave trade in 1807, and slavery proper in 1833. France abolished slavery in its colonies in 1848.
The Caribbean was known for pirates, especially between 1640 and 1680. The term "buccaneer" is often used to
describe a pirate operating in this region. The Caribbean region was war-torn throughout much of its colonial history,
but the wars were often based in Europe, with only minor battles fought in the Caribbean. Some wars, however, were
born of political turmoil in the Caribbean itself.
Decolonisation and modern period
In 1791, <color=#3366CC>a slave rebellion</color> in the French colony of Saint-Domingue led to the establishment in 1804 of <color=#3366CC>Haiti</color>, the first
republic in the Caribbean. Neighboring Santo Domingo (present-day <color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic</color>) would attain its
independence on three separate occasions in 1821, 1844 and 1865. Cuba became independent in 1898 following
American intervention in the <color=#3366CC>War of Independence</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Spanish-American war</color>. Following the war, Spain's last
colony in the Americas, <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, became an unincorporated territory of the United States. The U.S. also took
control of <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color>. The U.S., since the <color=#3366CC>Monroe Doctrine</color> in the 19th century, has excerted a major influence over the
Caribbean. The so-called <color=#3366CC>Banana Wars</color> in the early 20th century saw the temporary U.S. occupations of <color=#3366CC>Haiti</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic</color>.
Between the 1960s and '80s, most of the British holdings in the Caribbean achieved political independence, starting
with Jamaica in 1962, then Trinidad and Tobago (1962), <color=#3366CC>Guyana</color> (1966), Barbados (1966), <color=#3366CC>The Bahamas</color> (1973),

<color=#3366CC>Grenada</color> (1974), <color=#3366CC>Dominica</color> (1978), <color=#3366CC>St. Lucia</color> (1979), <color=#3366CC>St. Vincent and the Grenadines</color> (1979), <color=#3366CC>Belize</color> (1981) <color=#3366CC>Antigua and</color>
<color=#3366CC>Barbuda</color> (1981), and <color=#3366CC>St. Kitts and Nevis</color> (1983). In case of the Netherlands, the Netherlands Antilles received
autonomy status within the Kingdom in 1954, with Aruba receiving its own in 1986 and Curaçao and St. Maarten in
2010. Presently, the United States, Britain, France and the Netherlands still have some <color=#3366CC>Caribbean possessions</color>. During
the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, the U.S. would again intervene militarily into Caribbean countries including <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Dominican</color>
<color=#3366CC>Republic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Grenada</color>.
The decline of the export industries meant a need to diversify the economies of the Caribbean territories. The tourism
industry started developing in the early 20th century, rapidly developing in the 1960s when regular international flights
made vacations affordable and is now a $50 billion industry. Another industry that developed in the early 20th century
was offshore banking and financial services, particularly in The Bahamas and the <color=#3366CC>Cayman Islands</color>, as the proximity of
the Caribbean islands to North America made them an attractive location for branches of foreign banks seeking to avail
themselves of less complicated regulations and lower tax rates.
Geography
The geography and climate in the Caribbean region varies: Some islands in the region have relatively flat terrain of

non-volcanic origin. These islands include <color=#3366CC>Aruba</color> (which has minor volcanic features), <color=#3366CC>Curaçao</color>, <color=#3366CC>Barbados</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bonaire</color>, the
<color=#3366CC>Cayman Islands</color>, Saint Croix, <color=#3366CC>The Bahamas</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Antigua</color>. Others possess rugged towering mountain-ranges like the

islands of <color=#3366CC>Saint Martin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hispaniola</color>, <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jamaica</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dominica</color>, <color=#3366CC>Montserrat</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saba</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sint Eustatius</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saint</color>

<color=#3366CC>Kitts</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saint Lucia</color>, Saint Thomas, Saint John, Tortola, <color=#3366CC>Grenada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saint Vincent</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guadeloupe</color>, <color=#3366CC>Martinique</color> and <color=#3366CC>Trinidad</color>
<color=#3366CC>and Tobago</color>.
Definitions of the terms Greater Antilles and Lesser Antilles often vary. As part of the Puerto Rico Bank and the Puerto
Rico-Virgin Islands microplate, the Virgin Islands are sometimes included with the Greater Antilles. The term Lesser
Antilles is often used to define an island arc that includes Grenada but excludes Trinidad and Tobago and the Leeward
Antilles.
The waters of the Caribbean Sea host large, migratory schools of fish, turtles, and <color=#3366CC>coral reef</color> formations. The Puerto
Rico Trench, located on the fringe of the Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea just to the north of the island of Puerto
Rico, is the deepest point in all of the Atlantic Ocean.
The region sits in the line of several major shipping routes with the <color=#3366CC>Panama Canal</color> connecting the western Caribbean
Sea with the Pacific Ocean.
Climate

The climate of the area is <color=#3366CC>tropical</color>, varying from <color=#3366CC>tropical rainforest</color> in some areas to <color=#3366CC>tropical monsoon</color> and <color=#3366CC>tropical</color>
<color=#3366CC>savanna</color> in others. There are also some locations that are arid climates with considerable drought in some years, and
the peaks of mountains tend to have cooler <color=#3366CC>temperate climates</color>.
Rainfall varies with elevation, size and water currents, such as the cool upwellings that keep the <color=#3366CC>ABC islands</color> arid.
Warm, moist <color=#3366CC>trade winds</color> blow consistently from the east, creating both rain forest and semi arid climates across the
region. The tropical rainforest climates include lowland areas near the Caribbean Sea from <color=#3366CC>Costa Rica</color> north to <color=#3366CC>Belize</color>,
as well as the <color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, while the more seasonal dry tropical savanna climates are found in

<color=#3366CC>Cuba</color>, northern <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>, and southern <color=#3366CC>Yucatán, Mexico</color>. Arid climates are found along the extreme
northern coast of Venezuela out to the islands including <color=#3366CC>Aruba</color> and <color=#3366CC>Curaçao</color>, as well as the northwestern tip of
Yucatán.
While the region generally is sunny much of the year, the wet season from May through November sees more frequent
cloud cover (both broken and overcast), while the dry season from December through April is more often clear to
mostly sunny. Seasonal rainfall is divided into 'dry' and 'wet' seasons, with the latter six months of the year being wetter
than the first half. The air temperature is hot much of the year, varying from 25 to 33 C (77 F to 90 F) between the wet
and dry seasons. Seasonally, monthly mean temperatures vary from about 5 C (7 F) in the northern most regions, to
less than 3 C in the southernmost areas of the Caribbean.
Hurricane season is from June to November, but they occur more frequently in August and September and more
common in the northern islands of the Caribbean. <color=#3366CC>Hurricanes</color> that sometimes batter the region usually strike northward
of <color=#3366CC>Grenada</color> and to the west of Barbados. The principal hurricane belt arcs to northwest of the island of Barbados in the
Eastern Caribbean. A great example being recent events of Hurricane Irma devastating the island of Saint Martin
during the 2017 hurricane season.
Sea surface temperatures change little annually, normally running from 30 °C (87 °F) in the warmest months to 26 °C

to summer about 2–5 degrees on the southern islands and about a 10–20 degrees difference on the northern islands of
the Caribbean. The northern islands, like The Bahamas, Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic, may be
influenced by continental masses during winter months, such as cold fronts.

Biodiversity
The Caribbean islands have one of the world's most diverse ecosystems. The animals, fungi, and plants are
Conservation International biodiversity hotspots because of their exceptionally diverse terrestrial and marine
ecosystems, ranging from montane cloud forests to <color=#3366CC>tropical rainforest</color> to <color=#3366CC>cactus</color> <color=#3366CC>scrublands</color>. In the Caribbean, the area
of forest increased by 55,500 hectares per year in 1990–2000, 64,200 ha per year in 2000–2015 and 14,200 ha per
The region also contains about 8% (by surface area) of the world's coral reefs along with extensive seagrass meadows,
often found in the shallow marine waters bordering the region's island and continental coasts.
For the fungi, there is a checklist based on nearly 90,000 records derived from specimens in reference collections,
published accounts, and field observations. It includes more than 11,250 species of fungi recorded in the region. The
checklist is not exhaustive, and it is likely that the true number of fungal species already known in the Caribbean is
higher. The number of fungal species in the Caribbean, including species not yet recorded, is likely far higher, given the
generally accepted estimate that only about 7% of all fungi worldwide have been discovered. Estimates have been
made for endemic fungal species on some Caribbean islands. For Cuba, 2,200 species of fungi have been tentatively
identified as possible endemics of the island; for <color=#3366CC>Puerto Rico</color>, the number is 789; for the <color=#3366CC>Dominican Republic</color>, 699; for
Trinidad and Tobago, 407.
Many ecosystems in the Caribbean islands have been affected by <color=#3366CC>deforestation</color>, pollution, and human encroachment.
The arrival of the first humans is correlated with extinction of giant owls and dwarf ground sloths. The hotspot contains
dozens of highly threatened animals (birds, mammals, and reptiles), fungi, and plants. The threatened animals include
the Puerto Rican amazon, two species of <color=#3366CC>solenodon</color> (giant shrews) in Cuba and Hispaniola, and the Cuban crocodile.
The region's coral reefs, which contain about 70 species of hard corals and 500 to 700 species of reef-associated
fishes, have undergone rapid decline in ecosystem integrity and are considered vulnerable to global warming and
ocean acidification. According to a UNEP report, the Caribbean coral reefs might go extinct in next 20 years due to
human population explosion along the coastlines, overfishing, pollution of coastal areas, and global warming.
Some Caribbean islands have terrain that Europeans found suitable for cultivation for agriculture. <color=#3366CC>Tobacco</color> was an
important early crop during the colonial era, but was eventually overtaken by <color=#3366CC>sugarcane</color> production as the region's
staple crop. Sugar was produced from sugarcane for export to Europe. <color=#3366CC>Cuba</color> and <color=#3366CC>Barbados</color> were historically the largest
producers of <color=#3366CC>sugar</color>. The tropical plantation system came to dominate Caribbean settlement. Other islands were found
to have terrain unsuited for agriculture, for example <color=#3366CC>Dominica</color>, which remains heavily forested. The islands in the

southern <color=#3366CC>Lesser Antilles</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aruba</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bonaire</color> and <color=#3366CC>Curaçao</color>, are extremely arid, making them unsuitable for agriculture, but
they have salt pans that were exploited by the Dutch. Sea water was pumped into shallow ponds, producing coarse salt
when the water evaporated.
The natural environmental diversity of the Caribbean islands has led to recent growth in <color=#3366CC>eco-tourism</color>. This type of
tourism is growing on islands lacking sandy beaches and dense human populations.

Politics
Regionalism
Caribbean societies are very different from other Western societies in terms of size, culture, and degree of mobility of
their citizens. The current economic and political problems the states face individually are common to all Caribbean
states. Regional development has contributed to attempts to subdue current problems and avoid projected problems.
From a political and economic perspective, regionalism serves to make Caribbean states active participants in current
international affairs through collective coalitions. In 1973, the first political regionalism in the Caribbean Basin was
created by advances of the English-speaking Caribbean nations through the institution known as the Caribbean
Common Market and Community (<color=#3366CC>CARICOM</color>), in Guyana.
Certain scholars have argued both for and against generalizing the political structures of the Caribbean. On the one
hand the Caribbean states are politically diverse, ranging from socialist systems toward more capitalist
Westminster-style parliamentary systems. Other scholars argue that these differences are superficial, and that they
tend to undermine commonalities in the various Caribbean states. Contemporary Caribbean systems seem to reflect a
"blending of traditional and modern patterns, yielding hybrid systems that exhibit significant structural variations and
divergent constitutional traditions yet ultimately appear to function in similar ways". The political systems of the
Caribbean states share similar practices.
The influence of regionalism in the Caribbean is often marginalized. Some scholars believe that regionalism cannot
exist in the Caribbean because each small state is unique. On the other hand, scholars also suggest that there are
commonalities amongst the Caribbean nations that suggest regionalism exists. "Proximity as well as historical ties
among the Caribbean nations has led to cooperation as well as a desire for collective action". These attempts at
regionalization reflect the nations' desires to compete in the international economic system.
Furthermore, a lack of interest from other major states promoted regionalism in the region. In recent years, the
Caribbean has suffered from a lack of U.S. interest. "With the end of the Cold War, U.S. security and economic
interests have been focused on other areas. As a result there has been a significant reduction in U.S. aid and
investment to the Caribbean." The lack of international support for these small, relatively poor states, helped
regionalism prosper.
Following the Cold War another issue of importance in the Caribbean has been the reduced economic growth of some
Caribbean States due to the United States and <color=#3366CC>European Union</color>'s allegations of special treatment toward the region by
each other.
United States–European Union trade dispute
The Lomé Convention, which allowed <color=#3366CC>banana</color> exports from the former colonies of the Group of African, Caribbean and
Pacific states (ACP) to enter Europe cheaply, came into effect in 1976. In 1999, the United States under President <color=#3366CC>Bill</color>
<color=#3366CC>Clinton</color> launched a challenge in the <color=#3366CC>World Trade Organization</color> against the European Union over its preferential
program. The World Trade Organization sided in the United States' favour and the beneficial elements of the
convention to African, Caribbean and Pacific states have been partially dismantled and replaced by the Cotonou
Agreement.
During the US/EU dispute, the United States threatened to impose large tariffs on European Union goods (up to 100%)
to pressure Europe to change the agreement with the Caribbean nations in favour of the Cotonou Agreement.
Farmers in the Caribbean have complained of falling profits and rising costs as the Lomé Convention weakens. Some
farmers have faced increased pressure to turn toward the cultivation of illegal drugs, which has a higher profit margin
and fills the sizable demand for these illegal drugs in North America and Europe.
African Union relations
Many Caribbean nations have sought to deepen ties with the continent of <color=#3366CC>Africa</color>. The African Union-bloc has referred to
the Caribbean as the potential "Sixth Region" of the <color=#3366CC>African Union</color>. Some Caribbean states have already moved to join
Africa institutions including Barbados, Grenada, Guyana, and The Bahamas, which have all become members of the
African Export Import Bank. And the Caribbean Development Bank signing a cooperation strategic partnership
agreement with the African Development Bank (AfDB) At present Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Jamaica, Guyana,
and Suriname are at various stages of establishing direct air flights with Africa to boost person-to-person links and
boost trade between both regions.
The first inter-regional Africa-Caribbean Community (CARICOM) Summit took place in September 2021. In August
2023 the African Union's African Export–Import Bank officially opened its first Caribbean Community office in Barbados
beginning the process of integrating willing Caribbean states as the 6th region of the African Union.AFREXIMBANK
opens Caribbean office in Barbados
Caribbean Financial Action Task Force and Association of Caribbean States
Caribbean nations have also started to more closely cooperate in the Caribbean Financial Action Task Force and other
instruments to add oversight of the offshore industry. One of the most important associations that deal with regionalism
amongst the nations of the Caribbean Basin has been the Association of Caribbean States (ACS). Proposed by
CARICOM in 1992, the ACS soon won the support of the other countries of the region. It was founded in July 1994.
The ACS maintains regionalism within the Caribbean on issues unique to the Caribbean Basin. Through coalition
building, like the ACS and CARICOM, regionalism has become an undeniable part of the politics and economics of the
Caribbean. The successes of region-building initiatives are still debated by scholars, yet regionalism remains prevalent
throughout the Caribbean.
Bolivarian Alliance
The President of <color=#3366CC>Venezuela</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hugo Chavez</color> launched an economic group called the Bolivarian Alliance for the Americas
(ALBA), which several eastern Caribbean islands joined.

At the time of <color=#3366CC>European contact</color>, the dominant ethnic groups in the Caribbean included the <color=#3366CC>Taíno</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Greater Antilles</color>
and northern <color=#3366CC>Lesser Antilles</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Island Caribs</color> of the southern Lesser Antilles, and smaller distinct groups such as the
Guanajatabey of western Cuba and the Ciguayo of eastern Hispaniola. The population of the Caribbean is estimated to
have been about 750,000 before European contact. After contact, social disruption and epidemic diseases such as
smallpox and measles (to which they had no natural immunity) led to a decline in the Amerindian population, who were

replaced by groups such as the <color=#3366CC>Kongo</color>, <color=#3366CC>Igbo</color>, Akan, Fon, and <color=#3366CC>Yoruba</color>, as well as military prisoners from <color=#3366CC>Ireland</color>, who

were deported during the Cromwellian reign in <color=#3366CC>England</color>. Immigrants from <color=#3366CC>Britain</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color> also arrived, although the mortality rate was high for both groups.
The population is estimated to have reached 2.2 million by 1800. Immigrants from <color=#3366CC>India</color>, <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>, and other
countries arrived in the mid-19th century as indentured servants. After the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic slave trade</color> ended, the population
increased naturally. The regional population was estimated at 37.5 million by 2000.
In <color=#3366CC>Haiti</color> and most of the French, Anglophone and Dutch Caribbean, the population is predominantly of African origin; on
many of the islands/nations there are also significant populations of mixed racial origin (including Mulatto-<color=#3366CC>Creole</color>,
Dougla, <color=#3366CC>Mestizo</color>, Quadroon, Cholo, Castizo, Criollo, <color=#3366CC>Zambo</color>, Pardo, Chindian, Cocoa panyols, and Eurasian). On the

<color=#3366CC>Cayman Islands</color>, <color=#3366CC>Aruba</color> and <color=#3366CC>Belize</color> <color=#3366CC>mixed-race</color> people form the majority of the population. There are also populations of

European ancestry; <color=#3366CC>English</color>, <color=#3366CC>French</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>, <color=#3366CC>Italian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color> and <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> ancestry. <color=#3366CC>Asians</color>, especially those of
Chinese, Indian descent, and <color=#3366CC>Javanese</color> Indonesians, form a significant minority in parts of the region. Indians form a
plurality of the population in <color=#3366CC>Trinidad and Tobago</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guyana</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Suriname</color>. Most of their ancestors arrived in the 19th
century as indentured laborers.
The Spanish-speaking Caribbean populations are primarily of European, African, or racially mixed origins. Cuba has a
European majority, along with a significant population of African ancestry. Puerto Rico has a mixed race majority with a
mixture of European-African-Native American (tri-racial), and a large White and West African (black) minority. The
Dominican Republic has the largest mixed-race population, primarily descended from Europeans, <color=#3366CC>West Africans</color>, and
Amerindians.
The majority of <color=#3366CC>Jamaica</color> is of West African origin, in addition to a significant population of mixed racial background and
minorities of Chinese, Europeans, Indians, Indigenous, <color=#3366CC>Jews</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Arabs</color>. This is a result of years of importation of
slaves and indentured laborers, and migration. Most multi-racial Jamaicans call themselves either mixed-race or brown.

Similar populations can be found in the <color=#3366CC>Caricom</color> states of <color=#3366CC>Belize</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guyana</color>, <color=#3366CC>Suriname</color> and <color=#3366CC>Trinidad and Tobago</color>. <color=#3366CC>Trinidad</color>
<color=#3366CC>and Tobago</color> has a multiracial cosmopolitan society due to the arrivals of Africans, Indians, Chinese, <color=#3366CC>Arabs</color> and
Europeans along with the <color=#3366CC>native indigenous Amerindians</color> population. This multiracial mix has created sub-ethnicities
that often straddle the boundaries of major ethnicities, such as the Mulatto-<color=#3366CC>Creole</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mestizo</color>, Pardo, <color=#3366CC>Zambo</color>, Dougla,
Chindian, Afro-Asians, Eurasian, and Cocoa panyols.
Language
Spanish (64%), <color=#3366CC>French</color> (25%), English (14%), <color=#3366CC>Dutch</color>, <color=#3366CC>Haitian Creole</color>, and Papiamento are the predominant official
languages of various countries in the region. Almost every Caribbean country has a distinct <color=#3366CC>creole language</color> or dialect
that serves as its vernacular language. Most of these do not have official status, with the aforementioned Haitian Creole
and Papiamento as notable exceptions. Other languages such as Caribbean Hindustani, <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Javanese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Hmong</color>, Amerindian languages, other African languages, other European languages, and other Indian languages like
<color=#3366CC>Telugu</color> are also spoken.
Religion
<color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> is the predominant religion in the Caribbean (84.7%). Other religions in the region are Hinduism, <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Judaism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rastafari</color>, <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chinese folk religion</color> (incl. <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>), <color=#3366CC>Baháí</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jainism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color>,
Kebatinan, <color=#3366CC>Traditional African religions</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yoruba</color> (incl. Trinidad Orisha), Afro-American religions, (incl. <color=#3366CC>Santería</color>, Palo,
Umbanda, Brujería, Hoodoo, <color=#3366CC>Candomblé</color>, Quimbanda, <color=#3366CC>Orisha</color>, Xangô de Recife, Xangô do Nordeste, Comfa,
Espiritismo, Santo Daime, Obeah, Abakuá, Kumina, Winti, Sanse, Cuban Vodú, Dominican Vudú, Louisiana Voodoo,
<color=#3366CC>Haitian Vodou</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Vodun</color>).
